The Prophet was given concise speech, victory through awe and the keys of the world's treasures; after Heraclius reads his letter, Abu Sufyan sees the Byzantine king fearing him.
Asma ties the Prophet's emigration food with her belt; sacrificial meat and Sawiq serve as journey food, the Prophet blesses dwindling provisions, and a huge fish feeds 300 men.
Aisha, regretting she returns with Hajj only, is sent behind her brother Abdur-Rahman on his mount to perform Umrah from at-Tan'im while the Prophet waits.
Companions ride double: Anas behind Abu Talha, and Usama behind the Prophet on a donkey and on his camel at the Conquest, when he entered and prayed in the Ka'bah.
Each joint owes daily charity: judging justly, helping a rider mount or load up, a good word, steps to prayer and removing harm from the road all count.
The Prophet forbade travelling to a hostile country carrying copies of the Quran.
At Khaibar the people flee to their fort as the Prophet cries Allahu Akbar, Khaibar is ruined; later his announcer forbids donkey meat and the pots are overturned.
Going up they said Allahu Akbar and going down Subhan Allah, told not to shout to One who hears and is near; returning, the Prophet said they return repentant, worshipping.
A slave who falls ill or travels is rewarded like the good deeds he did at home in health, as Abu Burda tells Yazid, who fasted on journeys.
At the Trench Az-Zubair volunteers three times to scout the enemy, and the Prophet says every prophet has a disciple and his is Az-Zubair.
If people knew what the Prophet knew, none would travel alone at night; he sped on open ground, delayed Maghrib to join Isha when hurrying, and urged travellers home quickly.
Umar wanted to buy back cheaply a horse he gave for Allah's Cause; the Prophet forbade it, likening one who takes back his gift to a dog swallowing its vomit.
A man asks to join jihad; learning his parents are alive, the Prophet tells him to exert himself in their service.
On one of his journeys the Prophet sent a messenger ordering that no string or other necklace be left round camels' necks.
No man may be alone with a woman, nor a woman travel without a mahram; a man enlisted for a campaign is told to go on Hajj with his wife.
Ali, Az-Zubair and Al-Miqdad take Hatib's letter to Meccan pagans from a woman; Hatib says he sought protection for his family, and the Prophet spares him as a Badr fighter.
Among the Badr prisoners Al-Abbas was undressed, so the Prophet clothed him in Abdullah bin Ubai's shirt, which is why he gave Abdullah his own shirt.
At Khaibar the Prophet cures Ali's eyes, gives him the flag and tells him to invite them calmly to Islam, as guiding one person is better than red camels.
Allah wonders at people who will enter Paradise in chains.
Three get a double reward: a man who teaches, frees and marries his slave girl, a Scripture believer who accepts the Prophet, and a faithful slave.
Asked about night raids endangering pagan women and children, the Prophet says they are from them; finding a woman killed in a campaign, he forbids killing women and children.
Withdrawing an order to burn two men, the Prophet says only Allah punishes with fire; Ibn Abbas says he would have killed, not burnt, the people Ali burnt.
Ukl men, healed by camels' milk and urine, kill the shepherd, take the camels and leave Islam; caught, they have hands and feet cut, eyes seared, and die without water.
An ant bit a prophet, who had its colony burnt, and Allah rebuked him for burning a whole nation that glorifies Allah because one ant bit him.
Sent by the Prophet, who prays for him to sit firm on horses, Jarir leads 150 Ahmas horsemen to dismantle and burn Dhul-Khalasa, an idol house called the Yemeni Ka'bah.
The Prophet burnt the date-palms of Bani An-Nadir.
The Prophet sends Ansar men against Abu Rafi; Abdullah bin Atik slips into his fort at night, kills him and, despite a sprained foot, waits to hear him mourned.
Do not wish to meet the enemy but be patient on meeting it, Paradise being under swords' shade; Khosrau and Caesar will be ruined; and war is deceit.
The Prophet seeks someone to kill Ka'b bin Al-Ashraf, who hurt Allah and His Apostle; allowed to say what he likes, Muhammad bin Maslama talks with Ka'b, then kills him.
Hiding behind palms to hear Ibn Saiyyad murmur under a sheet, the Prophet says that had his mother not alerted him, the truth would have been clear.
At the Trench the Prophet carries earth until dust covers his chest hair, loudly reciting Abdullah bin Rawaha's verses asking Allah for calm and firm feet against the enemy.
The Prophet always received Jarir with a smile, and when Jarir said he could not sit firm on horses, struck his chest and prayed he be firm and rightly guided.
Ali brought water in his shield, Fatima washed the blood from the Prophet's face, and ash from a burnt palm mat was put into his wound.
Sending Mu'adh and Abu Musa to Yemen, the Prophet tells them to make things easy, give glad tidings rather than drive people away, love each other and not differ.
At Uhud archers leave their post for booty against orders, seventy Muslims are killed, and the Prophet has Abu Sufyan's boasts of Hubal and Al-Uzza answered.
The Prophet was the most generous and bravest; when Medina took fright at night he rode Abu Talha's unsaddled horse with his sword, telling people not to be scared.
Salama bin Al-Akwa cries for help, chases off Ghatafan and Fazara raiders with arrows and recovers the Prophet's she-camels; the Prophet tells him to forgive them.
Al-Bara says the Prophet did not flee at Hunain but, attacked by the pagans, dismounted proclaiming himself the Prophet, son of Abdul Muttalib; none was braver that day.
When Bani Quraiza accept Sa'd's judgement, Sa'd rules that their warriors be killed and their women and children taken prisoner, and the Prophet says he judged as Allah judges.
Entering Mecca in the year of the Conquest wearing a helmet, the Prophet is told Ibn Khatal clings to the Ka'bah's curtains and orders him killed.
